gaps.sentence: The programme ___ I watched last night was about volcanoes.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to things, even when it is the object of the clause.

gaps.sentence: I've told you everything ___ you need to know.
gaps.explanation: After 'everything', 'that' is used (and may be omitted); 'which' is avoided after 'everything'.

gaps.sentence: My laptop, ___ I bought only last year, has already crashed twice.
gaps.explanation: Non-defining clause about a thing: 'which', never 'that'.

gaps.sentence: They said nothing at all, ___ I found rather strange.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' here means 'and this'; it refers to the whole situation and follows a comma.

gaps.sentence: Pablo, ___ speaks five languages, works as an interpreter.
gaps.explanation: Non-defining clauses about people take 'who'; 'that' never follows a comma in standard English.

gaps.sentence: The new bridge, ___ cost two billion euros, opened last month.
gaps.hint: thing + extra information after a comma
gaps.explanation: 'Which' introduces non-defining clauses about things; 'that' is forbidden there.

gaps.sentence: The people ___ moved in upstairs are very quiet.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people; 'whose' would need a noun after it.

gaps.sentence: The scientist ___ research we cited has won the Nobel Prize.
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession: the scientist whose research…
